title: Resistance and resistivity

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What resistance is, how to use V = IR, and how the length, area and material of a wire set its resistance.

blocks.heading: Resistance
blocks.text: The resistance of a component is the ratio of the potential difference across it to the current in it: R = V/I. Its unit is the ohm (Ω). One ohm is the resistance of a component with a p.d. of one volt across it when the current in it is one ampere.

blocks.heading: Using V = IR
blocks.text: V = IR, with V the potential difference in volts, I the current in amperes and R the resistance in ohms. It holds for any component at any instant. For a component whose resistance changes, such as a filament lamp, it gives the resistance at that one current.

blocks.heading: Resistivity
blocks.text: The resistance of a uniform wire is R = ρL/A. ρ (rho) is the resistivity of the material, in Ω m; L is the length in metres; A is the cross-sectional area in m². A longer wire has more resistance, in proportion to its length. A thicker wire has less, and the area depends on the square of the diameter: A = πd²/4.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a copper extension lead
blocks.text: A copper wire in an extension lead is 2.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.50 mm². The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. First convert the area to m²: 0.50 mm² is 0.50 × 10⁻⁶ m², which is 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m². Then R = ρL/A = (1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 2.0) / (5.0 × 10⁻⁷). The top line is 3.4 × 10⁻⁸, and 3.4 ÷ 5.0 = 0.68, so R = 0.68 × 10⁻¹ Ω, which is 0.068 Ω. Two significant figures, like the data.

blocks.heading: Resistance is not the gradient
blocks.text: Resistance at a point on an I–V graph is V/I at that point. It is not the gradient of the line. A straight line that does not pass through the origin has a constant gradient, but V/I changes along it, so the resistance is not constant. Only a straight line through the origin shows a constant resistance.
